cards.front: What is the substitution method for solving recurrences?
cards.back: Guess a candidate asymptotic bound for $T(n)$, then prove the guess correct by induction on $n$.

cards.front: What is the first action performed in the substitution method?
cards.back: Guess the form of the solution (e.g., $T(n)\leq cn\log n$ or $T(n)=O(n^2)$).

cards.front: Apply substitution to prove $T(n)=T(n-1)+1$ is $O(n)$. State the inductive hypothesis.
cards.back: IH: assume $T(m)\leq cm$ for all $m<n$. Then $T(n)\leq c(n-1)+1=cn+(1-c)$. Choose $c\geq1$ so $1-c\leq0$.

cards.front: For $T(n)=2T(n/2)+n$, what candidate bound is guessed and why?
cards.back: Guess $T(n)=O(n\log n)$ because the recursion tree has $\log n$ levels each costing $n$.

cards.front: Complete the inductive step for $T(n)\leq cn\log n$ when $T(n)=2T(n/2)+n$ (assume $n>2$).
Why must the inductive hypothesis sometimes be strengthened when using substitution?
cards.back: To absorb lower-order terms (e.g., subtract $dn$ from the guessed bound) so the inequality holds for all $n$.

cards.front: How are base cases handled in a substitution proof?
cards.back: Choose constants $c$ and $n_0$ large enough that the claimed bound holds for all base cases $n\leq n_0$.
